---
# Equal Temperament

Ines Marchetti had been tuning pianos for forty-one years, and in that time she had learned that people rarely call a tuner because of the piano. They call because of the guest, the recital, the sale of the house, the child who has suddenly decided to take lessons. The piano itself has usually been out of tune for years, and nobody has minded. It is a patient instrument. It goes flat the way a tide goes out, so slowly that you can't point to the moment it happened.

The woman on the phone had said only, "It hasn't been touched in a long time. My granddaughter's coming in March."

"How long is a long time?"

A pause. "I'd have to think. Nineteen years? Twenty?"

"That's fine," Ines said. "I've seen worse. I once tuned one that had been in a barn."

"It's not in a barn," the woman said, and Ines heard in her voice the small stiffness of someone who has been made to feel inspected. "It's in the front room."

---

The house was on Alder Court, at the end, where the road gave up and became a gravel turnaround. It was a narrow two-story place with green shutters that needed paint and a porch swing hung from only one chain. Ines parked, gathered her case, and stood a moment breathing. Her knees were not what they had been. Neither were her hands, though she told no one about the hands. A slight tremor had come in the last two years, and it showed only when she held something out in front of her, a cup or a tuning fork. When she gripped the lever on a tuning pin it vanished, as if the work reminded her body of its manners.

The woman who answered the door was small and straight-backed, in a cardigan the color of oatmeal, with white hair pinned up in a way that suggested it had been pinned the same way every morning for decades. "Dorothea Vance," she said. "Thank you for coming out."

"Ines."

"The piano's through here. I should warn you, I haven't dusted it properly. I didn't like to move the things on top."

The things on top were photographs in frames, eleven of them, and a runner of yellowed lace, and a glass bowl with nothing in it. The piano was a Hazelton upright, dark walnut gone almost black, with brass sconces for candles that no one had lit in a century. Ines put her hand flat on the lid, an old habit, the way you might touch a horse's flank before you walked behind it.

"Lovely old thing," she said, and meant it.

"It was my husband's mother's. Then ours."

Ines set down her case and began to lay out her tools: the lever with its worn maple handle, the felt strips, the rubber wedges, the fork. She took off the fallboard and lifted the top. Dust lay across the strings like a fine pelt. She played a single A above middle C, and it came out sour and low, a bruised note, and then she played the octave below it and heard how far the two had drifted from each other.

"Well," she said. "It's flat."

"I thought it might be."

"Quite flat. I'd guess forty cents, maybe more. Nearly half a semitone." She played a few more notes, listening. "It's going to want to be pulled up before I can tune it properly. That's a bit of a process. There's some risk. Old strings sometimes don't like being asked to come back."

Dorothea folded her hands. "Will they break?"

"Maybe one or two. I'll go slowly. I'll do it in stages."

"All right," Dorothea said. She said it the way people sign forms. Then she went to the kitchen and Ines heard the tap run.

---

There is a fact about pianos that most people never learn, and it is the fact Ines loved most about her trade: no piano is ever perfectly in tune, and none can be. The mathematics won't allow it. If you tune a series of pure fifths, each one resonating cleanly with the note above it, and you stack twelve of them, you end up not quite where you started. The circle doesn't close. There is a small gap, called the Pythagorean comma, and it has troubled musicians for two and a half thousand years. Every solution is a compromise. You take the gap and spread it out, a sliver here and a sliver there, until every interval is slightly wrong and no interval is unbearable. This is equal temperament. It is why a piano can play in any key, and it is why every chord on a piano carries a faint, shimmering impurity that a violinist or a singer, free to adjust, would never permit.

Ines had explained this to clients maybe a thousand times, usually at the moment they asked why she was making the piano sound worse before she made it sound better. She'd play a third that was wide and beating, that pulsing wow-wow-wow that a tuner learns to count like a heartbeat, and say, "That's on purpose. That's what makes it work."

She had come to think it was less a technical fact than a moral one. Nothing holds together perfectly. What you can do is share the error fairly.

She began with the pitch raise, working from the bottom up, taking each string a little past where she wanted it so it would settle back. The lever bit into the pin, and she felt the old iron plate and the old wood take the strain. The piano complained in small clicks and pings. Halfway through the tenor section she heard the string before she felt it, the thin high snap, and a coil of wire sprang up and lashed across the back of her hand.

"Oh," said Dorothea from the doorway. She had returned without Ines noticing. "You're bleeding."

"It's nothing." It was a thin line, already beading. "That's one. I'm sorry. I'll replace it. I carry spare wire."

"Don't be sorry. I'm the one who let it go."

Ines glanced at her. Dorothea was not looking at the wire, or the hand. She was looking at the keyboard with a quiet, private fixity.

"Mrs. Vance—"

"Dorothea."

"Dorothea. Who played it, in the years before?"

There was a pause long enough that Ines began to regret the question. Then Dorothea came in and sat down on a straight chair by the window, with the winter light behind her.

"My husband, Arthur," she said. "Not well. He'd never had lessons. He'd learned some hymns from his mother and picked out songs from the radio. But he loved it. In the evenings he'd sit down and play, and I'd wash up and listen. And he sang. Terribly. He had a voice like a gate on a hinge." She almost smiled. "But he never sang a wrong note. Isn't that odd? He could hear exactly where the piano was, and he'd find it. When the piano went a bit flat, so did Arthur. He never noticed. He just followed it down."

Ines said nothing. She had learned that silence was one of the tools in her case.

"He died twenty years ago in October," Dorothea said. "And I closed the lid, and that was that. I never had it tuned. People suggested it. My daughter suggested it. I said I'd get to it."

"And now your granddaughter."

"Marguerite. She's nine. She plays the cello, actually, not the piano. But they have her learning piano too, for theory. She's coming to stay a month while her parents are abroad. I thought she'd want something to do." She looked at her hands. "I thought it would be nice if the house had music in it."

Ines went back to the pin. She did not say what she was thinking, which was that a house is a kind of tuning fork, and that this one had been sounding a single long flat note for twenty years.

---

It took two hours to bring the piano up to pitch, and it lost one more string, a bass-tenor unison she'd have to replace on a second visit. By the time she had the whole scale roughly where it belonged, the light in the window had gone from white to amber. Dorothea made tea and left it on the lid, on a saucer, and Ines drank it standing, then put down the cup, took up the fork, and struck it against her knee.

The fork gave its pure A, four hundred and forty cycles a second, thin and clear and without opinion. She set the first string of A4 against it and listened to the beats slow, and slow, and stop.

From there the work turned quiet and exact. She laid the temperament in the middle octave, muting the outer strings of each trio with felt so that she could hear one at a time, checking fourths against fifths, thirds against sixths, counting the beats. A good third in the temperament octave beats about seven times a second at the low end and speeds up as you climb; a good fifth beats slow, so slow it's like something breathing in its sleep. Ines had done this so many thousands of times that she no longer thought in numbers. She listened as one listens to a person who is nervous, waiting for the small tell.

When she reached the end of the octave she played the test: a slow progression through the keys, C major, then F, then B-flat, then E-flat, moving out into the sharps and flats where an ill-tempered piano shows its teeth. The chords opened like doors, one after another, each with its faint shimmer.

She realized Dorothea had gone very still.

"Is that—" Dorothea began, and stopped.

"That's it in tune. Or in temper, I should say. There's more to do, I have to bring in the rest of the range and then go around again, because the tension shifts as I go. But that's roughly where it should be."

Dorothea was pressing her lips together. "It sounds so *bright*."

"It does, after a long flat spell. The ear adapts. It gets used to the low. Then it's like someone opening a curtain."

"It doesn't sound like Arthur's piano."

Ines turned on the bench. Dorothea's face was doing something complicated. It was not grief exactly, more the look of a person who has walked into a familiar room and found the furniture moved an inch.

"No," Ines said gently. "I don't suppose it does."

"I keep hearing it wrong. I keep thinking, that's not the note." She laughed, a dry small sound. "Which is absurd. I know it's the right note. I know that's what it's *supposed* to sound like. But for twenty years I've—" She waved a hand at the piano, the room, the air. "I've been keeping the sound of it in my head. Him singing along, flat. And now it's *correct*, and he's not in it anymore."

Ines had, over the years, been asked many things in people's living rooms. She had been asked to appraise, to repair, to lie about the value of an heirloom. She had never quite been asked this. She thought about what the honest answer was, and what the kind one was, and whether they were the same.

"I could put it back," she said.

Dorothea looked at her.

"Not all the way. I couldn't get it to where it was, exactly. It wasn't a stable flat, it was just where it drifted to, and it's not that anymore now that I've moved the strings. But I could leave it lower. A few cents, maybe a quarter-tone. It would be playable. It wouldn't be wrong, exactly, just low. Some people prefer it, actually, on old instruments. Easier on the plate." She paused. "But it would be out of pitch with anything else. A cello, for instance. If Marguerite wanted to play the two together, she'd have to retune her strings to match, or they'd fight."

"She'd hate that."

"She'd be nine. She'd probably just be confused."

Dorothea took a long breath. She looked at the photographs on the lid, the eleven faces, and then at the keys. "It's a strange thing to be sentimental about," she said. "A wrong note."

"I don't think it's strange," Ines said. "I think a lot of what we love is wrong notes. The little ways someone's off from the standard. Your husband found the note the piano was actually on. That's not nothing. Most people sing to where it's supposed to be."

"That's kind."

"It's just accurate. I hear a lot of people sing."

They sat in the amber light. Somewhere in the walls, the furnace ticked on.

"Would you play something?" Dorothea said suddenly. "Not the test. Something. So I can hear it as a piano and not a job."

Ines hesitated. She was a tuner, not a pianist. She had learned enough to test an instrument, scales and chords and a few pieces that showed off a piano's registers. But she turned back and thought for a moment, and then, unbidden, her hands found the opening of a hymn. It was one of the ones everyone's mother seems to have known, plain and rocking in three-four time. She hadn't played it in decades. She played it slowly, with the tremor gone from her fingers as it always went, and the chords rose into the room, slightly impure and entirely alive, the thirds wide and shimmering, the whole beautiful compromise of it.

By the second verse, Dorothea was singing.

Her voice was thin and true. It was nothing like a gate on a hinge. She sang the words softly, with her eyes closed, and when the hymn ended Ines let the last chord ring until it died in the wood.

"Well," Dorothea said, and wiped her cheek with the back of her wrist. "That's all right, isn't it. That's all right."

"It is."

"Leave it as it is. Finish the way you were going to. Marguerite should have a piano that agrees with her cello." She smiled. "Arthur would have followed it anywhere. He'd have found the note."

---

Ines finished after dark. She went around the whole range a second time, then a third, tightening the unisons until each trio sang as one string, and the room filled with the clean hum of an instrument at rest. She replaced the broken string on the spot after all, because she had wire in the case and the bass didn't feel right without it. She wiped the dust from the keys with a damp cloth, and did not touch the photographs.

At the door, Dorothea paid her in cash from an envelope and then, after a moment, added a little more.

"That's too much."

"It isn't. I'd like you to come back in the fall. They say you should, don't they? Twice a year?"

"Once is enough for most. Twice if you play a lot."

"Then twice," Dorothea said. "If Marguerite plays a lot."

Ines nodded. She stepped out onto the porch and the cold hit her face. The swing moved slightly on its one chain in the wind. Behind her, through the door Dorothea had not yet closed, she heard a single note, a soft tentative A above middle C, struck by one finger, and then held, and let go.

It was exactly on pitch. It hung in the house a moment, bright and unafraid, and Ines, who had heard that note perhaps a million times in her life, stopped on the step to listen to it fade.

Then she went down to the car, and her hands, on the wheel, were steady.
---

Its resolution favors accepting the piano’s new pitch while preserving the past in a shared song, rather than restoring the old sound.

Medium — The story’s recurring tuning metaphor and its patient, craft-specific attention make its themes and emotional resolution unusually coherent and distinctive.
